extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of public administration and administrative law
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize the defining features, statutory triggers, and procedural requirements of formal (hearing) rulemaking in U.S. public administration, distinguishing it from informal and hybrid rulemaking. Useful for understanding when agencies must use on-the-record hearings and what procedures those hearings entail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of administrative rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal rulemaking is one of three forms of administrative rulemaking in the United States: informal (notice and comment), hybrid, and formal (hearing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entry classifies rulemaking into three discrete procedural types to frame when different processes apply; this taxonomy is the starting point for determining applicable procedural rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of formal rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal rulemaking involves agencies holding hearings – on the record and presided over by an administrative law judge – to adjudicate a rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that formal rulemaking is an adjudicative, record-based proceeding with an ALJ presiding; the hearing itself is the central procedural mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigger: undue effect on life or livelihood of a small group
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal rulemaking is used to adjudicate a rule when that rule unduly affects the life or livelihood of a small group of individuals or organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion explains when the more rigorous procedural protections of formal hearings are warranted—where rules have concentrated, significant effects on a defined small group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal rulemaking does not require “notice and comment” as the hearing serves this purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that the administrative hearing in formal rulemaking performs the informational and adversarial functions that notice-and-comment procedures provide in informal rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required civil-procedure mechanisms (cross-examination; ALJ judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal rulemaking does require most of the mechanisms of civil law procedure including cross-examination and the judgment of an administrative law judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies key procedural features to be present in formal rulemaking hearings—e.g., adversarial testing of evidence through cross-examination and adjudication by an ALJ—distinguishing it from non-adversarial procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory prompt: 'on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing'
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal rulemaking is prompted when the authorizing legislation stipulates agencies are required to promulgate rules 'on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies the canonical statutory phrasing that mandates formal rulemaking; use of this specific statutory language generally triggers the requirement for on-the-record hearings.
